questions.q: What are the four column categories a well-designed dimension table sorts into?
options: Surrogate key, natural key, descriptive attributes, and foreign keys to other dimensions
Primary key, foreign key, index, and constraint
Row number, timestamp, checksum, and version
Fact key, measure, aggregate, and filter
questions.explain: A dimension table's columns fall into four groups: its own surrogate key, the natural key traceable to the source system, descriptive attributes used for filtering and grouping, and (when relevant) foreign keys to other dimension tables.

questions.q: Why is it acceptable — even correct — for a dimension table to be denormalized?
options: Dimension tables have relatively few rows, so the storage cost of redundant data is small compared to the query-performance benefit
Denormalization is never acceptable in any warehouse table
Dimension tables don't actually store any redundant data
Denormalization makes writes faster, which is all a dimension table needs
questions.explain: Because dimensions are small relative to fact tables, flattening hierarchy levels onto one row costs very little storage but avoids extra joins on every analytical query.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what word in a stakeholder's request is the practical tell for a needed dimension attribute?
options: "By" — as in "sales by region, by month"
"Total"
"Average"
"Report"
questions.explain: Whenever someone says they need to analyze something "by" some property, they're naming a dimension attribute your table needs to support that filter or group-by.

questions.q: How does a dimension table's typical row-and-column shape compare to a fact table's?
options: A dimension table is wide but short (many columns, few rows); a fact table is narrow but tall (few columns, many rows)
Both are always exactly the same shape
A dimension table is narrow but tall, and a fact table is wide but short
Dimension tables never have more than one column
questions.explain: Dimension tables carry rich descriptive detail across relatively few rows, while fact tables stay narrow (mostly keys and measures) but can grow to billions of rows.

questions.q: Which columns in a dimension table are typically NOT aggregated (summed, averaged) in an analytical query?
options: Descriptive attributes — they're used to filter and group, not to be added up
Every column in the table, including the surrogate key
Only the natural key column
None — dimension attributes are always summed
questions.explain: Descriptive attributes provide context for slicing and grouping fact data; the numbers meant to be summed live in the fact table's measure columns instead.
